chunks.title: This Website — Architecture & Tech
chunks.tags: site website portfolio how built made technology stack architecture special unique framework vanilla javascript html css
chunks.content: Built with Claude Code (main features) and OpenCode (maintenance). Each page is a standalone HTML file with vanilla JavaScript, a shared CSS design system (Deep Sea Terminal theme), and Google Fonts, served as static files on GitHub Pages. The homepage fish canvas is a layered steering system: an eight-level behavior priority stack running edge avoidance, heading commitment, state behaviors, collision, schooling, and wander in order; three size classes with distinct behavior; V-formation schooling with stable slot assignment; and a breadth-first navigation field so fish route around drawn walls instead of only steering off them. The design page runs the same engine under a blueprint canvas that recognizes drawn shapes and turns them into walls and obstacles. Search is three tiers over a precomputed index: BM25 keyword retrieval with field boosting, a semantic layer using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings quantized to int8 and fused with the keyword results by reciprocal rank, then optional generation either in-browser through WebGPU or against a local LMStudio or Ollama endpoint. Results render as one adaptive surface whose density follows how specific the query was. Other features: shape-based geometric navigation, an infinite-canvas playground with pan and zoom, a cosmos starfield on the art page, and a search overlay on every page via Cmd-K.
chunks.micro: Static HTML per page, vanilla JS, built with Claude Code.
chunks.tldr: Standalone HTML + vanilla JS on GitHub Pages — a layered fish steering system, a shape-recognition canvas, and a three-tier search that runs an LLM in the browser.

chunks.title: AI Search System
chunks.tags: search AI LLM qwen webgpu lmstudio ollama minisearch bm25 browser local model inference
chunks.content: Three-tier search with progressive enhancement. Tier 1: MiniSearch BM25 instant keyword search, always on. Tier 2: Qwen 3.5 (0.8B parameters) running entirely in-browser via WebGPU and Transformers.js — no server needed. Tier 3: auto-detects local LMStudio or Ollama models on localhost for higher quality answers. Also supports custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Engine color coding: WebGPU blue, LMStudio purple, Ollama orange, Custom green. AI can be toggled on or off by the user.
chunks.micro: BM25 → WebGPU Qwen → your local model.
chunks.tldr: Three tiers: instant BM25, in-browser Qwen 3.5 on WebGPU, and auto-detected LMStudio/Ollama — user-toggleable.

chunks.title: JHDesign Review Canvas — Design Review Tooling
chunks.tags: review canvas tooling design review iframe grid focus git multiplayer collaborative ratings comments annotation openprose internal tool built
chunks.content: The JHDesign Review Canvas is a tool John built to review dozens of live website experiments at once. It shows the contents of a repo as one navigable page with three view modes, canvas, grid and focus, where every page is a live iframe with star ratings, typed comments, and freehand drawings composited onto screenshots. Review state lives in git and each reviewer writes only their own file, so feedback merges without conflict and needs only a GitHub repo to be collaborative. A display cut of it is embedded at the end of the OpenProse case study.

chunks.title: Handling Disagreement
chunks.tags: disagreement disagreed disagree conflict pushback overruled convinced advocacy stakeholders engineering compromise authority product decisions collaboration
chunks.content: Does the best design available at the level of authority he has, and advocates for what he thinks is best for the product. Works with engineering to think through ways to make a thing easier to build while still getting what the user needs, rather than handing over a spec and walking away. Treats compromise as a forcing function: simplifying down to the core requirement is often where the innovation actually shows up. Will defer on the genuinely impossible, but not before the options are exhausted.
chunks.micro: Advocate hard, defer only to the impossible.
chunks.tldr: Does the best design available at his level of authority and advocates for the product — treats compromise as a forcing function toward the core requirement.

chunks.title: Ambiguity and Constraint
chunks.tags: ambiguity structure standards scoping constraints timeline cuts prioritization process design thinking
chunks.content: Ambiguity is where he works best. He is always looking for structure, including the unspoken structure inside processes everyone already considers settled, and generates standards as they are needed. He deliberately revisits ambiguity even after a project has been iterated into a narrow scope, to keep it in mind that everything could still change. That pays off when a timeline is cut in half: he usually already knows what will have to go before anyone asks, and can keep paring if it halves again.
chunks.micro: Thrives in ambiguity; already knows what goes first.
chunks.tldr: Looks for structure everywhere, including the unspoken kind inside settled processes — and keeps ambiguity live even on tightly scoped work.

chunks.title: Critique and Design Reviews
chunks.tags: critique design review feedback how might we solutionizing stakeholders roast facilitation shared understanding
chunks.content: Runs critique playfully, leaning on open-ended "how might we" statements to avoid solutionizing, where a design gets taken too literally too early. Sets expectations going into any review, manages stakeholders, and levels with peers. Keeps the work outside himself — any given iteration is just the best current approach, so he does not get attached and enjoys a good roast. The best products stand up to scrutiny, so he invites it. He invites people to see the potential while giving concrete answers, and guides the room away from simple yes or no toward shared understanding, so the best outcome emerges from critique as a process rather than surviving it.
chunks.micro: Invite the roast. The work is not you.
chunks.tldr: Runs critique playfully and open-ended, steering away from yes/no toward shared understanding so the outcome emerges from the process.

chunks.title: Research That Changed the Design — Nanome
chunks.tags: user research usability testing qualitative coding pharmaceutical scientists VR navigation spotlight follow teleportation pivot evidence
chunks.content: On Nanome 2 he designed the test criteria and ran multiple rounds of usability testing with real pharmaceutical user groups, both existing Nanome 1 users and new ones. To make sense of feedback from scientists with different backgrounds he used qualitative data coding, sorting responses into actionable bugs, "how might we" explorations, evidence supporting features, and usability patterns, so the team could prioritize meaningfully. The first rounds confirmed the new aesthetic was appreciated but showed VR navigation was still hard — one tester: "Still have trouble with moving around the structure and other users." He led a fundamental pivot, removing teleportation-based navigation entirely and introducing the Spotlight/Follow paradigm, a non-rivalrous approach adapted from 2D tools into XR that lets collaborators share focus while still exploring independently. It became one of Nanome 2 signature features.
chunks.micro: Testing killed teleportation. Spotlight/Follow replaced it.
chunks.tldr: Multi-round testing with pharma users, coded qualitatively, produced a navigation pivot that became one of Nanome 2’s signature features.

chunks.title: Working with AI
chunks.tags: AI agentic design practice claude code verification QA steering vibe coding prototyping workflow definitions expectations
chunks.content: Treats AI as the ultimate omni-developer that is perhaps a bit too obedient, which makes clear definitions and expectations the designer’s job. Builds systems to verify output rather than simply trusting it. Sees AI as a middle zone between direct hand manipulation, like drawing and Figma, and passive vibe coding, and prefers intentional steering. Coming from a decade-long design career, the practice inverted: where he used to build a design up from reference and pastiche toward the requirements, he now generates candidates that already meet the requirements and pares them down, which is closer to sculpting than painting. QA became the thing he will not compromise on, and it stays manual. He has always held that a designer should know every screen and every state, and that matters more now that AI can build so much so fast — so go and test it.
chunks.micro: An omni-developer that is a bit too obedient.
chunks.tldr: Treats AI as an omni-developer that needs definitions, expectations and verification systems — steering deliberately rather than vibe coding.

chunks.title: Failure and Resilience
chunks.tags: failure resilience avatarmedic pivot funding startup lifeguard rescue perspective lessons consultancy
chunks.content: AvatarMEDIC was ambitious and too early, underfunded, and eventually his own capital was exhausted. He gave up the fundraising product dream and pivoted the company into a consultancy that brought in revenue. He holds that failures are the lead of golden wisdom: transmuting the lesson is what makes a person more resilient. His first job was lifeguarding, dealing with life and death directly. He has saved lives, including being first on scene for a c-spine injury and working large surf rescues, alongside the preventative work that makes up most of the job. That gives him a gradient of failure uncommon in tech: life or death is the only real failure, and as long as you are breathing you can try again.
chunks.micro: Life or death is the only real failure.
chunks.tldr: AvatarMEDIC was too early and underfunded; he pivoted it into a revenue-earning consultancy. A lifeguarding background sets his gradient of failure.

chunks.title: What John Is Looking For
chunks.tags: hiring availability full time lead designer senior designer founding designer opportunities roles startups consulting coaching
chunks.content: Seeking full-time work and open to projects, with a bias toward full time. Interested in innovative startups in their early stages, in work for established companies where an orthogonal thinker is useful, and in continuing to coach. Lead Designer or Senior Designer; founding designer for the right team. He is looking for unique opportunities that call for a generalist’s range with a specialist’s depth, and offers a founder’s experience with an IC’s ruthlessness and a Director’s vision.
chunks.micro: Seeking full-time, open to projects.
chunks.tldr: Seeking a full-time role, with a bias toward full time, and open to projects — Lead or Senior Designer, founding designer for the right team.
